morph.note: Gerundive of √वच् (वच् + tavya, with c → k): ‘she is to be told’. The person told is the grammatical subject, as with verbs of speaking in the passive.
Absolutive of √गम् (the m drops before -tvā). Its doer is the messenger, who is also the logical agent of वक्तव्या and of कार्यम् (त्वया).
Present of √इ ‘go’ (एति) with the prefix अभि ‘towards’: ‘comes to (me)’. Present tense after यथा for a purpose: ‘so that she comes’.
Gerundive of √कृ with the affix ṇyat and vṛddhi (कार्-य): ‘to be done’, used impersonally with the agent त्वया.

mantras.anvaya: (त्वया) गत्वा मम वचनात् सा ‘इति च इति च’ वक्तव्या; यथा च (सा) सम्प्रीत्या अभ्येति, तथा त्वया लघु कार्यम्।
mantras.anvaya_en: Śumbha’s instructions in two passive sentences built on gerundives: वक्तव्या (‘she is to be told’) and कार्यम् (‘it is to be done’), the second with a यथा … तथा clause of purpose.
mantras.lit: Having gone, she is to be told on my word such-and-such; and so that she comes with good will, so is it to be done by you, quickly.
mantras.tr: ‘Go to her and tell her this and this from me; and act quickly, so that she comes to me willingly.’
mantras.tr_note: The gerundives are rendered as imperatives addressed to the messenger, which is their force.

comm.t: Śumbha’s instructions to Sugrīva, given without a speaker label: speak to her on my authority, and bring her quickly and willingly. इति च इति च stands for the message itself, which the envoy delivers in full in 5.106–114.
A modern reading: Śumbha wants her consent (सम्प्रीत्या, ‘gladly’) but only as a means — ‘arrange it so that she comes’. Courtesy put to the service of possession is still possession.

mantras.anvaya: सः, यत्र अतिशोभने शैलोद्देशे सा देवी आस्ते, तत्र गत्वा, ततः तां मधुरया गिरा श्लक्ष्णं प्राह।
mantras.anvaya_en: Main clause सः … प्राह; an absolutive (तत्र गत्वा) with a relative clause of place (यत्र … आस्ते) whose subject सा देवी stands in the second line.
mantras.lit: He, having gone there where that Devī was staying, on a most beautiful region of the mountain, then spoke to her gently with sweet speech.
mantras.tr: Sugrīva went to the lovely mountain slope where the Goddess was staying, and addressed her gently, in honeyed words.
mantras.tr_note: The kept reading places सा देवी, the subject of the relative clause, in the second line; the translation brings it back into that clause.

comm.t: The envoy reaches the Goddess on the mountain and speaks to her softly. His gentleness belongs to the instructions he was given (5.103: bring her ‘with good will’).

Text: GRETIL and Freund read तां च देवीं ततः प्राह ‘and then he spoke to that Devī’, which makes the second line a simple object clause. The Gita Press reading सा देवी तां ततः प्राह is kept here, with सा देवी as the subject of यत्रास्ते and तां resuming her as the person addressed (corrections.json, variants: ‘Textual Verification Required’).

flags.uncertain: Variant reading: the Gita Press has सा देवी तां ततः प्राह; GRETIL and Freund have तां च देवीं ततः प्राह. The kept reading is construed with सा देवी as the displaced subject of यत्र आस्ते; it is grammatical but unusual in order, and the other reading is smoother. Status in corrections.json: Textual Verification Required.

mantras.anvaya: देवि, दैत्येश्वरः शुम्भः त्रैलोक्ये परमेश्वरः (अस्ति)। तेन प्रेषितः दूतः अहं त्वत्सकाशम् इह आगतः (अस्मि)।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two nominal sentences with the copula understood: Śumbha’s status, then the messenger’s own (अहम् with दूतः, प्रेषितः, आगतः).
mantras.lit: O Devī, Śumbha, lord of the daityas, is the supreme lord in the three worlds. I, a messenger sent by him, have come here into your presence.
mantras.tr: ‘Goddess, Śumbha, lord of the demons, is supreme sovereign of the three worlds. I am his envoy, sent by him, and have come here before you.’

comm.t: Sugrīva opens with protocol: he names his master’s title and his own office. Śumbha is called परमेश्वरः, ‘supreme lord’, in the three worlds.
The title is ironic in context: the gods’ hymn has just praised the Goddess as the power within all beings, and the one being addressed as ‘Devī’ is the true sovereign the envoy does not recognise.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) names the Goddess परमेश्वरी (name 396), the feminine of the title Śumbha claims here. The comparison is ours; the Devī Māhātmya itself makes the irony through its story.
